title: Detecting Anomalies in Karst Aquifer Recharge: A Temporal Convolutional AutoEncoder Framework With High‐Frequency Temperature‐Conductivity Signals
content:
Abstract

The internal recharge dynamics of karst aquifers are difficult to resolve with traditional outlet-based indicators, owing to their heterogeneous structure and nonlinear response. To address this, we propose a non-invasive anomaly detection framework based on a Temporal Convolutional AutoEncoder (TCAE), which integrates high-frequency electrical conductivity (EC) and temperature (T) signals to characterize recharge mechanisms. The study was conducted in a karst basin in Guilin, China, using 15-min EC, T, and rainfall data from three spring types: conduit-dominated, fracture-matrix mixed, and shallow-fracture controlled. The model accurately reconstructed non-event EC across sites (R 2 = 0.980–0.998) and quantified rainfall-triggered anomalies using peak (AEpeak) and cumulative (AEAUC) anomaly energy. AEpeak showed strong internal consistency with event-scale EC change (r = 0.897–0.923), while AEAUC was significantly correlated with cumulative outlet-discharge response (r = 0.590–0.857). Mixed-effects analysis of Ca2+ and HCO3 − concentrations, together with environmental isotope evidence from δ 13CDIC, 222Rn, and δ 18O, provided complementary support for the physical interpretation of AE-based recharge-type classification. Recharge events were classified into four types based on the maximum event-scale changes in EC and T: cold dilution, warm dilution, cold concentration, and warm concentration. Kruskal–Wallis test, and K-means clustering revealed distinct patterns across spring types: rapid recharge in conduit systems, buffered responses in fracture-matrix systems, and threshold activation in shallow fracture systems. This study presents the first application of TCAE in karst hydrology. The dual-parameter EC–T framework offers a real-time, high-resolution, and low-cost tool for characterizing dynamic recharge, supporting sustainable management and early warning in karst aquifers.
